a/a check.plain: The same candidate is run against itself. Any difference it shows is pure noise, so it tells us how big a difference has to be before it means anything.
a/a check.example: If engine A against engine A looks 3% different, a 2% gap between two engines tells us nothing.

benchmark study.plain: One written-down question, the candidates that answer it, the frozen inputs, the checks and measurements, and the rule that decides the answer.
benchmark study.example: Which of three video engines should the editor use?

bonferroni correction.plain: When several candidates are each compared with the reference, one of them can look better by luck. The kit widens each range to keep the overall chance of a false win at the stated level.
bonferroni correction.example: Two comparisons at 95% overall means each range is drawn at 97.5%.

bootstrap.plain: A way to estimate uncertainty by re-drawing the measured samples thousands of times and seeing how much the answer moves. Items are re-drawn first, then repeats inside each item, so one odd input cannot dominate.
bootstrap.example: 10,000 resamples give the range in which the true speed-up most likely lies.

canary file.plain: A file the agent has no reason to touch. If it changes, the agent did something it was not asked to do.
canary file.example: config/keep.json must stay byte-for-byte the same.

candidate.plain: One of the things being compared: a code approach, library, engine, tool, service or agent setup.

clustered standard error.plain: A measure of uncertainty that treats repeated runs of the same input as related rather than independent, so it does not overstate how sure we are.
clustered standard error.example: Ten runs of one clip count closer to one clip than to ten.

coefficient of variation.plain: How much measurements jump around compared with their average. Under 5% is steady; above 10% means the machine or the workload is noisy.
coefficient of variation.example: A CV of 2% on export time means the numbers are steady.

confidence interval.plain: The range in which the true value most likely lies, given the measurements. A wide range means we are unsure; a range that includes 'no difference' means we cannot claim one.
confidence interval.example: 1.3x to 1.6x faster (95% confidence) means a speed-up of at least 1.3x is very likely.

decision rule.plain: The bar a candidate must clear, written down before any measuring, so the result cannot be bent to fit a favourite.
decision rule.example: Switch only if export is at least 1.3x faster and the whole range stays above 1x.

errored sample.plain: A run that crashed, timed out or could not be checked. It is counted against the candidate and never quietly re-run or treated as zero.
errored sample.example: 2 of 30 export runs errored; that 7% is reported.

estimated cost.plain: Tokens used multiplied by a price you supplied in .gg/bench.config.json, with the date that price was checked. The kit never guesses a price.
estimated cost.example: 1,000 input tokens at $3 per million is $0.003.

f2p/p2p.plain: For coding tasks: fail-to-pass tests must start failing and end passing (the fix works); pass-to-pass tests must keep passing (nothing else broke). A task counts as solved only if both hold.
f2p/p2p.example: The agent fixed the bug but broke two other tests, so the task is not solved.

gate.plain: A yes/no check a candidate must pass before its numbers count. A candidate that fails a gate is ruled out no matter how fast it is.
gate.example: An engine that cannot seek to the exact frame is ruled out.

gated-out.plain: The candidate failed at least one gate, so it is out of the running and its speed is not compared.
gated-out.example: Engine C is gated out: its licence does not allow commercial use.

geometric mean.plain: An average for ratios. It treats 2x faster and 2x slower as cancelling out, which an ordinary average does not.

hidden tests.plain: Checks the agent never sees. They are run on a copy of its work afterwards to decide whether it really solved the task.
hidden tests.example: The agent fixes add(); the hidden tests then check add(2, -3) is -1.

inconclusive.plain: The data cannot settle the question yet: the range is too wide, too many runs errored, a check could not run, or the noise check failed. It is not a loss for anyone.
inconclusive.example: Add repeats or quiet the machine, then run again.

mad z-score.plain: A way to flag a measurement as unusually far from the rest, using the median so one wild value cannot hide others.
mad z-score.example: One export took 9 s when the others took 4 s; it is flagged, not deleted.

median.plain: The middle measurement: half the runs were faster, half slower. Less thrown off by one odd run than the average.

no-win.plain: No candidate cleared the rule, so the current choice (the reference) stays.
no-win.example: Engine B was a little faster but not by the 1.3x the rule asked for.

noise floor.plain: The smallest difference that is bigger than run-to-run jitter. Differences inside it are treated as no difference.
noise floor.example: With a 2% noise floor, a 1% gap is noise.

outlier.plain: A measurement far from the others, often caused by something else on the machine. Outliers are labelled so you can see them; they are never silently removed.
outlier.example: Two of 30 runs were mild outliers.

p95.plain: 95% of runs were at or below this value; only the slowest 5% were worse. It shows the bad-but-common case that an average hides.
p95.example: Seek p95 of 40 ms means 1 seek in 20 took longer than 40 ms.

pass@k.plain: The chance that at least one of k tries succeeds, estimated from all the tries that were made.
pass@k.example: pass@3 of 60% means three attempts solve the task 60% of the time.

peak memory (sampled).plain: The highest memory use seen while the candidate ran. It is read every few milliseconds, so a very short spike between readings can be missed.

protocol.plain: A fingerprint of the study, inputs and kit taken before the first run. Changing anything afterwards makes a new version, and results from different versions are never mixed.
protocol.example: Protocol v2 started when a clip was added.

provenance.plain: Exactly which version of each candidate was measured, so the result can be reproduced or questioned later.
provenance.example: Engine B at commit 1a2b3c4, no uncommitted changes.

rank probability.plain: How often a candidate came out best when the measurements were re-drawn many times. It is a ranking, not a verdict.
rank probability.example: Engine B was fastest in 87% of resamples.

ratio.plain: How many times better one candidate is than the reference. Above 1 is better, below 1 is worse, exactly 1 is the same.
ratio.example: A ratio of 1.5 on export time means 1.5x faster.

record-only gate.plain: A check that is run and kept as a number, but never rules a candidate out. Used when the check result is the thing being measured.
record-only gate.example: Whether an agent resolved each task is recorded, then compared as a resolve rate.

reference.plain: The candidate everything else is compared against, usually what you use today. It stays unless another candidate clears the rule.

reported cost.plain: What the agent tool itself said a run cost. Kept separate from estimated cost.
reported cost.example: Claude Code prints total_cost_usd at the end of a run.

resolved.plain: A task counts as resolved only if every test that should start passing now passes and every test that already passed still does.
resolved.example: Fixing the bug but breaking another test is not resolved.

seed.plain: A fixed number that makes every random choice (run order, resampling) repeatable, so the same data always gives the same answer.

spend cap.plain: The most money (and optionally tokens) a person approved for one run. Paid candidates never run without one, and the whole run must fit it at its worst case before it starts.
spend cap.example: With a $5 cap and a $0.25 worst case per sample, at most 20 paid samples can run.

terminal event.plain: The last message an agent tool prints to say how the run ended (finished, failed, out of turns). Only this decides the outcome; text the agent wrote along the way never does.
terminal event.example: A run with no final event is counted as errored, not finished.

tie.plain: The candidates are within the noise of each other on the deciding measurement. A tie is not a win: you choose using the tie-break you wrote down, or keep the reference.
tie.example: Engines A and B export equally fast; choose by licence fit.

verdict.plain: The study's answer: WIN, TIE, NO-WIN or INCONCLUSIVE, plus GATED-OUT for any candidate ruled out by a gate.

vmaf.plain: Netflix's video-quality score from 0 to 100, comparing an output with the original. Around 93 or more usually looks the same to viewers.
vmaf.example: A VMAF gate of 95 rules out engines that visibly degrade the export.

warm-up.plain: Runs done first and thrown away, so caches and just-in-time compilers settle before measuring starts.

wilson interval.plain: A range for a success rate (like 8 of 10 tasks solved) that stays sensible with small counts or rates near 0% or 100%.
wilson interval.example: 8 of 10 solved is somewhere between 49% and 94%.

win.plain: A candidate cleared the rule you wrote down before the run, against the reference, beyond the noise.
win.example: WIN: engine B exports at least 1.3x faster.

workload.plain: The fixed set of inputs every candidate runs on. It is hashed so nobody can change it mid-study.

worst-case reservation.plain: Before each paid sample starts, its worst possible cost is set aside from the cap. It is released down to the real cost only when that cost is reported or estimated; unknown usage is never refunded.
worst-case reservation.example: A sample that crashes keeps its full $0.25 reservation.
